Glucose rules stop applying on this phone until it is connected again.
Paste the access token on its own, without spaces.

This removes the whole group and everything inside it. This can’t be undone.
Start from something that fits your family, or build the rule yourself.

⚠ Update every phone before using the new rule features

%1$s may be running an app version older than %2$s. Rules with several actions, an exception or an “at least” group only work on %2$s or later. An older child’s phone ignores them, and deletes them on its next sync. Update every phone in the family first.
⚠ Rules are about to be lost: update every phone now

This family already has rules that need %2$s or later, and %1$s may be running an older version. An older child’s phone does not enforce those rules, and deletes them on its next sync. Update every phone in the family now, then check that the rules are still there.

What the rule does while its condition holds. Allow beats a block; always block beats an allow; exempt entirely beats even an always block. Set a limit replaces the target’s own daily allowance — the tighter limit wins.
What this rule acts on: the whole device, chosen apps or categories, or everything except a short list you choose.
The phone counts a device as near while it is connected over Bluetooth — a car, headphones, or another phone. Pair it first, then paste its Bluetooth address here.
After some minutes of screen time
This rule stops applying straight away, on every phone that has it. This can’t be undone.

Requests that this answered automatically will wait for a parent again. This can’t be undone.
Sent — takes effect once the child\'s phone syncs.
Sent — the child\'s phone drops the rule once it syncs.

This rule blocks every app, always, and nothing else in this ruleset lets any app through. Nothing will run until this rule is turned off, deleted, or changed. If you meant to allow a few apps through, add an Allow rule for them first.

This rule always-blocks every app, always, and an Allow rule cannot free anything from it — only Exempt entirely can, and nothing else in this ruleset uses that. Nothing will run until this rule is turned off, deleted, or changed. If you meant to spare a few apps, add an Exempt entirely rule for them first.
A place is saved from where you are standing. Coordinates stay on this phone: they are never sent anywhere and never appear in the log.
No location available yet. Open a maps app for a moment, then try again.

Asked the phone to add this place. It will appear here once confirmed.
Which apps you open and for how long, your total screen time each day, and which rules applied. This is worked out on the phone and kept on the phone.
Your messages, your photos, what you type, what is on your screen, your location, your browsing, and the contents of any app. None of it is read, stored or sent.

Only when you ask for more time, or when a request is answered. What is sent: how many minutes were asked for, what for, the reason you wrote, and whether the answer was yes or no. Nothing else — no app list, no screen time, no location. Every message is encrypted on this phone first, so the server cannot read any of it.
Nothing. Sending to parent phones is turned off, so this phone talks to no server at all.

A short record of what the app did — that it checked your time, that it started, that something failed. It holds no app names, no reasons you wrote and no times you were using anything. You can read all of it.

A parent can ask this phone to send a copy of the log above, so they can check on a problem without holding this phone. It only happens when asked for, never automatically, and it is exactly the log shown here — nothing more.
Dementor Watch log. Contains only what the app did: event names, counts and times. No app names, no messages, no reasons, no passwords.
This erases everything recorded so far, including the last error below if there is one. It cannot be undone.

Enforcement failed to run and is retrying on its own. This is the technical detail behind that — it can mention a rule, category or place name, unlike the log above. Only shown here, and included if you share the log.

A category’s limit covers its own apps plus every app in whatever is nested inside it, all the way down — nesting Games inside Fun means Fun’s one limit covers both without re-listing every app. An app counted through two different paths only spends the budget once. Today\'s total, how much of the limit is left, and the five apps you used most, with how long each was open. No times, no history of when you used anything, and nothing about what you did inside an app. Your parents see the same numbers you see on this phone — nothing more.

This suspends every browser on the phone that these filters cannot apply to, the moment you turn it on. Whoever is holding the phone will notice at once.

Some of what this app does needs Android’s permission, and the switches are not where you would expect. Here is each one, what it is for, what it lets this app see, and where the switch is.
What Android has to allow, and where the switches are
These paths are Android’s. Samsung, Xiaomi and others rename the screens — if a heading here does not match, look for the same words nearby.
The one this app cannot work without. It is how screen time is measured at all — without it nothing is counted and no limit can apply.

What it allows: seeing which apps are opened and for how long. Not what is done inside them, and not what is on the screen. Android keeps this switch well hidden because an app that has it can watch how a phone is used — which is exactly what this app does, with both of you able to see the result.

Every rule is built from the same three parts: a condition (when), an effect (what it does), and a target (who). These examples show what different combinations actually add up to.
Make sure one app is never blocked
An allow always beats a block from a different rule, so this app stays reachable even if a category it belongs to gets blocked elsewhere.
Block a whole category, except one app
Two rules working together: the category block and the app-specific allow. The excepted app may belong to the blocked category — the allow still wins.
Keep one app blocked even though its category is allowed

The mirror image of the pair above: always block beats an allow from a different rule, for the one app in an otherwise-fine category that must stay off no matter what. Only Exempt entirely could free it now.
Lock the phone down to just the essentials during school hours
“Everything except” is the strict version of a schedule: instead of naming what to block, you name the short list that should keep working, and everything else stops.
Give more time on weekends than school nights
One rule can carry a different number of minutes for different days — no separate weekday and weekend rules needed.
Block games only on the school Wi-Fi during school hours
“All of these” means every condition has to hold together — being on that Wi-Fi on a weekend evening would not be enough on its own.
Relax the rules at Grandma’s, or whenever Dad’s phone is nearby
“Any of these” means one condition holding is enough — the two situations do not need to happen at the same time.
Keep the emergency contact app reachable no matter what
Exempt entirely is the strongest tier of all — it beats even an always-block override — and unlike a plain allow, it also holds against network and DNS blocking, not just other rules.
